questions.qtext:
An organisation has been allocated the IP address block $140.25.0.0$. The goal is to divide this address block into multiple subnets, each capable of supporting at least 25 hosts.
Which of the following subnet masks should be used to create subnets that meet this requirement while minimising address space wastage?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 7)
An A / 27 subnet provides 32 total IP addresses, of which 30 are usable (excluding the network and broadcast addresses). This subnet size is the smallest that can accommodate 25 hosts with minimal address wastage.
Source solution 2 (score: 3)

We need subnets that support at least 25 usable hosts and minimise wasted addresses. For a prefix /m, usable hosts = 2^(32−m) − 2

A. /25 → 2^7 − 2 = 126 (meets requirement, but wastes many addresses.)

B. /26 → 2^6 − 2 = 62 (meets requirement, still has excess.)

C. /27 → 2^5 − 2 = 30 ✔︎ (meets requirement and is smaller (less waste) than /26 or /25.)

D. /28 → 2^4 − 2 = 14 (does not meet the 25-host requirement.)

Thus the smallest mask that gives ≥25 usable hosts is /27 (255.255.255.224).

Source solution 3 (score: 1)
Option A, B, C gives us the desired result of getting at least 25 ip addresses for the host.

But we need to select the subnet mask which minimises the address wastage which is our Desired condition from the question.

Option C has less ip addresses wastage. Because the network part is /27 so we have 5bits (2^5= 32 host ip addresses) for host and then usable host ip addresses are 32-2=30.
So the wastage is atmost 5 host ip addresses. Which is less compared to option A and B.

Therefore answer option C.

questions.qtext:
A company is assigned three IP address blocks: $149.16.23.0/22$, $149.16.24.0/22$, and $149.16.30.0/22$.
It wants to divide these blocks into 12 equal-sized subnets for internal use. What subnet mask should be assigned to each of the 12 subnets?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 14)
Each / 22 block can be split into four / 24 subnets. Three blocks give $3 \times 4=12$ subnets.
Source solution 2 (score: 10)

The company has been assigned three IP address blocks: 149.16.23.0/22, 149.16.24.0/22, and 149.16.30.0/22.

  • The block 149.16.23.0/22 corresponds to the network 149.16.20.0/22 (range: 149.16.20.0 to 149.16.23.255).

  • The block 149.16.24.0/22 is a valid network address (range: 149.16.24.0 to 149.16.27.255).

  • The block 149.16.30.0/22 corresponds to the network 149.16.28.0/22 (range: 149.16.28.0 to 149.16.31.255).

These three blocks are contiguous and cover the range from 149.16.20.0 to 149.16.31.255, providing a total of 3072 addresses (3 × 1024 addresses per /22 block).

The company wants to divide these blocks into 12 equal-sized subnets. Each subnet should have 3072 / 12 = 256 addresses. A subnet with 256 addresses requires a /24 subnet mask (255.255.255.0), as a /24 block provides exactly 256 addresses.

Each /22 block can be divided into 4 /24 subnets:

  • 149.16.20.0/22 divided into /24 subnets: 149.16.20.0/24, 149.16.21.0/24, 149.16.22.0/24, 149.16.23.0/24.

  • 149.16.24.0/22 divided into /24 subnets: 149.16.24.0/24, 149.16.25.0/24, 149.16.26.0/24, 149.16.27.0/24.

  • 149.16.28.0/22 divided into /24 subnets: 149.16.28.0/24, 149.16.29.0/24, 149.16.30.0/24, 149.16.31.0/24.

This results in exactly 12 equal-sized subnets, each with a /24 mask.

Thus, the correct subnet mask for each subnet is /24.

Answer: C./24

questions.qtext:
You are asked to allocate a subnet from the block $214.97.254.0/17$ that can provide exactly 2 usable host IP addresses.
Which of the following subnet assignments is most suitable?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 8)
A /30 subnet provides 4 IPs total: 2 usable host IPs, 1 network address, and 1 broadcast.
Source solution 2 (score: 1)
Answer option A.

For option A we have 30bits for the network out of 32 bits,which means we have 2 bits for the host part.

Now coming to the host part 2 bits we can have 4 ip addresses. In those 4 ip addresses they asked for only USABLE means we need to subtract those ip which cannot be given to the hosts as ip address.

The ip addresses that are not used as ip addresses for hosts are subnet id and DBA. So we need to subtract these 2 ip addresses out of 4 ip addresses.

Finally we are left with 2 usable host ip addresses. Which is a desirable condition in the question.
Source solution 3 (score: 1)
Option A: 214.97.254.4/30

/30 ⇒ 232−30=42^{32-30}=4232−30=4 total addresses

2 reserved (network + broadcast)

Usable hosts = 4−2=24-2=24−2=2

Subnet:

  • Network: 214.97.254.4
  • Hosts: 214.97.254.5, 214.97.254.6
  • Broadcast: 214.97.254.7

Exactly 2 usable hosts.

Option B: 214.97.254.0/29
  • /29 ⇒ 23=82^3=823=8 total addresses
  • Usable hosts = 8−2=68-2=68−2=6

Too many hosts.

Option C: 214.97.254.2/31
  • /31 ⇒ 2 addresses total.
  • Traditionally no usable hosts (network and broadcast).
  • Although modern point-to-point links can use /31, in subnetting questions the expected answer is usually not /31 for host allocation.

Not the standard answer.

Option D: 214.97.254.0/28
  • /28 ⇒ 24=162^4=1624=16 total addresses
  • Usable hosts = 16−2=1416-2=1416−2=14

Too many hosts.

questions.qtext:
A company has been assigned a Class C IP address and decides to use $\mathbf{6}$ bits for subnetting.
How many usable host addresses per subnet are available?
questions.solution:
Answer: 2

Source solution 1 (score: 5)
A Class C address has 8 bits for host addressing.

If 6 bits are used for subnetting, only $8-6=2$ bits remain for host addresses.

Total host addresses per subnet: $2^{2}=4$
Usable host addresses $=2^{2}-2=2$

Correct Answer: 2 usable host addresses per subnet
Source solution 2 (score: 1)
Answer 2
Given class c network which means we will have 24bits for the network out of 32. Finally we are left out with 8bits(32-24=8). These 8bits will be host part.

They also gave that 6 bits for subnetting. Subnetting means we need to borrow bits from the host.which means out of 8 bits left, we need to take 6bits for subnetting. So we are left with 2 bits. Finally we have 2 bits for host part.

Now for 2 bits we can have 4 ip addresses. i.e,(2^2=4).

From the total of 4 ip addresses usable addresses are only 2 because, we cant use network id(1st ip) and DBA(last ip) as host ip addresses so these 2 were also subtracted from 4 ip addresses.

Finally the usable host addresses per subnet are only 2.

questions.qtext:
A company uses part of the $214.97.254.0/17$ block.
The subnet $B$ is allocated $214.97.254.0/25$, and $214.97.254.0/29$ is reserved for internal routing.
How many usable addresses are left in Subnet B for host assignments?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 11)
From /25 (128 addresses), subtracting /29 (8 addresses) leaves 120 addresses for use.



$128-8(/ 29$ block $)-1($ network ID of $/ 25)=119$
Source solution 2 (score: 1)
1. Total Addresses in Subnet B

Subnet B is defined as 214.97.254.0/25.

  • A /25 mask leaves $32 - 25 = 7$ bits for hosts.

  • Total IP addresses = $2^7 = 128$.

2. Subtracting the Reserved Internal Block

The problem states that 214.97.254.0/29 is reserved for internal routing.

  • A /29 mask covers $2^3 = 8$ addresses.

  • These 8 addresses (from .0 to .7) are "taken" from Subnet B's pool.

  • Remaining: $128 - 8 = 120$.

3. Why subtract that final 1?

Usually, we subtract 2 for any subnet: one for the Network ID and one for the Broadcast Address.

  • The Network ID: The network ID for Subnet B is 214.97.254.0. Notice that this address is already included in the 8 addresses we subtracted for the /29 block. Therefore, we don't need to subtract it again.

  • The Directed Broadcast Address: Every subnet needs a broadcast address (where all host bits are 1). For a /25 network starting at .0, the broadcast address is 214.97.254.127. This address is not part of the reserved /29 block, so it must be subtracted separately to find the "usable" host addresses.

  • Total Pool: 128 addresses (.0 through .127).

  • Step A (Reserved Block): You remove the 8 addresses (.0 through .7) for internal routing.

    • Result: $128 - 8 = 120$.

    • Crucial Note: Since .0 was part of that 8-address block, the Network ID is already gone.

  • Step B (The DBA): The broadcast address for a /25 starting at .0 is .127. This address was not in the .0 to .7 range, so it is still sitting in your remaining pool of 120. You must subtract it now.

    • Final Result: $120 - 1 = 119$.

The Final Formula:

$$\text{Usable Addresses} = (\text{Total in B}) - (\text{Reserved Block}) - (\text{Broadcast Address})$$

$$128 - 8 - 1 = 119$$

Source solution 3 (score: 0)
This question is beautiful because the entire network 214.97.254.0/29 is reserved for internal routing so no of ips in this network =8

and 1 ip for direct broadcast addreess so from 128-8-1=119

chance of silly mistake taking single ip instead of network.
Source solution 4 (score: 0)

it is a very good question

Source solution 5 (score: 0)

Given:

  • Subnet B = 214.97.254.0/25
  • Internal routing subnet = 214.97.254.0/29 (carved out of Subnet B)

Step 1: Total addresses in Subnet B (/25)

Host bits = 32 − 25 = 7
Total addresses = 2⁷ = 128
Range: 214.97.254.0 – 214.97.254.127

Step 2: Usable addresses in a /25 (before considering the /29)

Every subnet reserves 1 address for Network ID and 1 for Broadcast.
Usable = 128 − 2 = 126

Step 3: Addresses consumed by the /29 internal routing block

Host bits = 32 − 29 = 3
Total addresses in /29 = 2³ = 8
Range: 214.97.254.0 – 214.97.254.7

Note: 214.97.254.0 is already excluded in Step 2 (it's Subnet B's network address), so only the remaining 7 addresses (214.97.254.1 – 214.97.254.7) need to be additionally removed from the usable pool.

Step 4: Final usable addresses for host assignment

126 − 7 = 119

Answer: 119

questions.qtext:
An organisation has been allocated the IP block $10.0.0.0/24$ to set up a subnet LAN1 that must support 40 hosts, including space for a network address, a broadcast address, and one router interface.
Two subnetting strategies are considered:

  • Method 1: Use a single subnet of size /26, which allocates 64 IP addresses.
  • Method 2: Split LAN1 into two smaller subnets: one subnet with 32 addresses (/27) and one subnet with 16 addresses (/28)

Which of the following statements is correct regarding address utilisation?

options.text: Method 1 is more efficient because it uses a single continuous block of 64 addresses.
Method 2 is invalid since subnets of this size $/ 27$ and $/ 28$ cannot coexist in the same /24 block.
Both methods are equally efficient since both satisfy the 40-host requirement.
Method 2 is more efficient, as it allocates only $32+16=48$ addresses instead of 64.

questions.solution:
Answer: D

Source solution 1 (score: 8)
Method 1: Uses a /26 subnet

$$
2^{6}=64 \text { addresses allocated }
$$
Method 2: Uses a /27 and a /28 subnet
$$
2^{5}+2^{4}=32+16=48 \text { addresses allocated }
$$

Since both methods provide sufficient usable hosts, Method 2 is clearly more efficient in terms of address utilisation, as it minimizes unused IPs.
Source solution 2 (score: 5)

Question Analysis:

  • Requirement: Support 40 hosts, plus 1 network address, 1 broadcast address, and 1 router interface.

    • Total IPs needed $\approx 40 \text{ (hosts)} + 3 \text{ (overhead)} = 43$.

  • Method 1: Use a single subnet of size /26.

    • A /26 block has $2^{(32-26)} = 2^6 = \mathbf{64}$ addresses.

    • This is sufficient to hold 43 IPs.

    • Allocated size: 64 addresses.

  • Method 2: Split LAN1 into two subnets: one of size /27 and one of size /28.

    • A /27 block has $2^5 = 32$ addresses.

    • A /28 block has $2^4 = 16$ addresses.

    • Allocated size: $32 + 16 = \mathbf{48}$ addresses.

    • Capacity check:

      • Subnet 1 (/27): 32 IPs - 3 overhead = 29 hosts.

      • Subnet 2 (/28): 16 IPs - 3 overhead = 13 hosts.

      • Total Host Capacity = $29 + 13 = 42$ hosts.

      • Since $42 > 40$, this method can physically support the required number of hosts.

Evaluation of Options:

  • A. Method 1 is more efficient because it uses a single continuous block of 64 addresses.

    • Incorrect. Efficiency in IP addressing is usually defined by minimizing wasted addresses. Allocating 64 addresses when fewer would suffice is generally considered less efficient.

  • B. Method 2 is invalid since subnets of this size /27 and /28 cannot coexist in the same /24 block.

    • Incorrect. Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) allows subnets of different sizes to coexist within a larger parent block without issue.

  • C. Both methods are equally efficient since both satisfy the 40-host requirement.

    • Incorrect. While both satisfy the requirement, one consumes 64 addresses from the organization's pool while the other consumes only 48. They are not equally efficient in terms of usage.

  • D. Method 2 is more efficient, as it allocates only $32 + 16 = 48$ addresses instead of 64.

    • Correct. By using VLSM (Method 2), the organization only needs to set aside a total of 48 IP addresses to meet the demand, whereas Method 1 forces them to burn a block of 64. Therefore, Method 2 saves 16 IP addresses ($64 - 48$), making it more efficient in terms of address utilization.

Answer:

The correct option is D.
